messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The “standard deviation” you’re looking for is the standard error of the sample mean under the null hypothesis.  
It’s calculated as:

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

where  
\(s = 1.4\) (sample standard deviation)  
\(n = 40\) (sample size)

\[
SE = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249} \approx 0.2215
\]

So the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis is **≈ 0.22**.  

*(If you were instead asking for the standard deviation of the test statistic itself, that would be 1 for a t‑distribution with 39 degrees of freedom.)*
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test. That likely refers to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis. The standard error is sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That is indeed the standard error: sigma / sqrt(n). They gave sample_std_dev = 1.4. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40). sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. So 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2215. So about 0.2215.

But they might want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test statistic? The test statistic is (sample_mean - population_mean) / (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). The denominator is the standard error. So the standard deviation of the test statistic under the null is 1 (if using t distribution with df=39). But they might want the standard deviation of the null distribution of the sample mean. That is the standard error. So answer: about 0.2215.

Thus we can respond: The standard error of the mean under the null is 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 0.2215. If you want the standard deviation of the test statistic, it's 1 (for t distribution). But likely they want the standard error. So answer accordingly.
